name: Peter Martyr Vermigli
role: Italian Reformed theologian; professor at Strasbourg, Oxford, and Zürich

died.cause: Fever (illness), after returning from the Colloquy of Poissy

summary: A leading Italian Augustinian canon who embraced Protestant teaching, fled the newly refounded Roman Inquisition in 1542, and became one of the most respected Reformed theologians of his day. He taught at Strasbourg, at Oxford under Edward VI, where he helped shape the English Reformation and defended the Reformed view of the Lord's Supper, and at Zürich. His Loci Communes became a standard Reformed textbook.

key_dates.label: Professes as an Augustinian canon of the Lateran congregation; studies at Padua
Becomes prior of San Pietro ad Aram in Naples, where he joins the reform-minded circle of Juan de Valdés
Becomes prior of San Frediano in Lucca and introduces reforms in teaching and preaching
Summoned by his order amid suspicion of heresy as the Roman Inquisition is refounded; flees to Zürich and then Strasbourg
Marries Catherine Dammartin, a former nun, in Strasbourg
Invited to England by Archbishop Cranmer; becomes Regius Professor of Divinity at Oxford (1548)
Oxford disputation on the Eucharist, defending a Reformed understanding of Christ's presence
After Mary I's accession is held under house arrest, then allowed to leave England; returns to Strasbourg
Becomes professor of Hebrew at Zürich, succeeding Konrad Pellikan
Attends the Colloquy of Poissy in France with Theodore Beza

accomplishments.text: Became one of the most influential Reformed theologians of the sixteenth century; his commentaries and treatises were collected after his death as the Loci Communes (1576), widely used as a Protestant textbook, especially in England.
Defended a Reformed doctrine of the Lord's Supper, that Christ is truly received by faith but not physically present in the bread, in the 1549 Oxford disputation and later writings.
Advised Cranmer on the English Reformation, influencing the 1552 Book of Common Prayer and working on the draft revision of church law (Reformatio legum ecclesiasticarum).
Combined Aristotelian scholastic training with Reformed theology, helping to shape later Reformed scholasticism.
Was a skilled Hebraist and wrote biblical commentaries on Judges, Kings, Romans, and 1 Corinthians, among others.
Taught reformist ideas to his community at Lucca, many of whose members later left Italy for Protestant cities.

persecuted_others_note: Vermigli did not order or carry out persecution. Like most Reformers, he held that Christian magistrates should restrain heresy, and he worked on the draft English church-law code that proposed severe penalties for heretics; it was never enacted.

persecuted_others.title: Draft church-law code with penalties for heresy
persecuted_others.summary: He served on the commission, led by Cranmer, that drafted the Reformatio legum ecclesiasticarum, which provided for heretics who refused to recant to be handed over to the civil authorities for punishment. Parliament never passed it.

persecution_note: Vermigli fled Italy to escape the Roman Inquisition and was later forced out of England under Mary I; Catholic authorities in Oxford also exhumed and desecrated his wife's body.

persecution.title: Flight from the Roman Inquisition
persecution.summary: Suspected of heresy for his teaching at Lucca, he was summoned to appear before his order's chapter at Genoa just as Pope Paul III refounded the Roman Inquisition. Fearing arrest, he fled Italy in August 1542.

responsible.name: Superiors of the Lateran Canons
responsible.role: Summoned him to answer for his teaching
responsible.jurisdiction: Order of Canons Regular of the Lateran

responsible.name: Pope Paul III and the Roman Inquisition
responsible.role: Re-established the Inquisition (July 1542) to pursue heresy in Italy

persecution.outcome: He reached Zürich and then Strasbourg; he never returned to Italy.

persecution.title: House arrest under Mary I
persecution.summary: When Mary I restored Catholicism, Vermigli was confined in Oxford and then in London under house arrest before being allowed to leave England, a release often credited to his status as a foreigner.

responsible.name: Mary I and her council
responsible.role: Restored Catholic worship and restricted Protestant leaders

persecution.outcome: Allowed to leave for Strasbourg; his colleague Cranmer was later burned.

persecution.title: Exhumation of his wife's body
persecution.summary: Commissioners sent by Cardinal Reginald Pole to Oxford had the body of his wife, Catherine Dammartin, who had died there in 1553, dug up from Christ Church cathedral and buried in a dunghill as the remains of a heretic's wife. Under Elizabeth I in 1561 her bones were reburied mixed with the supposed relics of St Frideswide.

responsible.name: Cardinal Reginald Pole
responsible.role: Archbishop of Canterbury and papal legate whose commissioners visited Oxford

persecution.outcome: Her remains were later reburied in the cathedral.

excommunication_note: Vermigli abandoned his religious order and the Catholic Church in 1542 and was treated by Rome as a heretic. His works were banned in the first class of the Index of Prohibited Books, which forbade all of an author's writings.

excommunications.reason: Listed among authors whose entire works were forbidden
excommunications.status: The Index was abolished in 1966; never formally revoked for him

sources.citation: Josiah Simler, Oration on the Life and Death of Peter Martyr (1563), in Peter Martyr Vermigli, Life, Letters, and Sermons, ed. and trans. John Patrick Donnelly. Peter Martyr Library, vol. 5. Kirksville, MO: Thomas Jefferson University Press, 1999.
